claim: Transcranial calcium imaging of the AC of an anesthetized GCaMP6s mouse following repeated presentations of a 5 kHz-37 dB SPL pure tone revealed cortical activity in three distinct areas: the primary AC (A1), secondary AC (A2), and anterior auditory field (AAF).
source: Transcranial calcium imaging of the AC of an anesthetized GCaMP6s mouse following repeated presentations of a 5 kHz-37 dB SPL pure tone (Figure 1A) revealed cortical activity in three distinct areas, the primary AC (A1), secondary AC (A2), and anterior auditory field (AAF), consistent with previous work (Issa et al., 2014; Figure 1B, MATLAB code in Figure 1—source code 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo calcium imaging (Figure 1A, 1B) and is consistent with previous work cited (Issa et al., 2014).

claim: Across 40 trials of the same sound presentation, A1 showed either a full population response (population ON cortical responses) or no response (population OFF cortical responses).
source: Across the 40 trials of the same sound presentation, we observed that A1 showed either a full population response (here called population ON cortical responses) or no response (referred to here as population OFF cortical responses), with some variability within each class (Figure 1C, MATLAB code in Figure 1—source code 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging across multiple trials (Figure 1C).

claim: The responses to sound stimuli were independent of stimulus presentation order.
source: Inspection of the individual cortical responses over time revealed the responses to be independent of stimulus presentation order (Figure 1D, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing temporal patterns of responses (Figure 1D).

claim: A histogram of Δf/f of sound-evoked calcium signals from A1 across trials showed two classes of A1 responses ('Population ON' vs. 'Population OFF').
source: Collectively, a histogram of Δf/f of sound-evoked calcium signals from A1 across trials showed two classes of A1 responses ('Population ON' vs. 'Population OFF,' Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from histogram analysis (Figure 1E).

claim: A greater frequency of population ON cortical responses was observed with increasing sound pressure level.
source: A greater frequency of the population ON cortical responses was observed with increasing sound pressure level (Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between sound pressure level and response frequency (Figure 1F).

claim: Similar stochastic population sensory cortical responses have been observed previously.
source: Similar stochastic population sensory cortical responses have been observed previously (MacLean et al., 2005; Kenet et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2014; Sakata and Harris, 2009), but the mechanisms that determine whether a population ON or OFF response occurs have not yet been elucidated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the IC evoked neuronal activity in the IC, MGB, TRN, and AC as indicated by stimulus-evoked flavoprotein autofluorescence (FA) and calcium-dependent fluorescence signals.
source: The auditory colliculo-thalamocortical (aCTC) mouse brain slice retains the synaptic connections between these structures: hence, electrical stimulation of the IC evoked neuronal activity in all of these brain structures as indicated by stimulus-evoked flavoprotein autofluorescence (FA) and calcium-dependent fluorescence signals (Figure 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FA and calcium imaging in brain slices (Figure 2A-E).

claim: Individual time series of stimulus-evoked FA and calcium signals across trials of IC stimulation reveal stochastic responses in the AC, despite MGB, TRN, and IC being always responsive to IC stimulation.
source: However, review of the individual time series of Δf/f of the stimulus-evoked FA and calcium signals across trials of IC stimulation (Figure 2C and E, Figure 2—source data 1 and 2) reveals stochastic responses in the AC; a pattern that was similar to the in vivo data, despite the fact that MGB, TRN, and IC were always responsive to IC stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from FA and calcium imaging across multiple trials (Figure 2C, 2E).

claim: Whole-cell recording from MGB and TRN cells showed spikes in response to each stimulus irrespective of the presence of a population AC response.
source: This finding was consistent with whole-cell recording from MGB and TRN cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), where spikes were seen in response to each stimulus irrespective of the presence of a population AC response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).

claim: FA and calcium signals from the MGB are smaller than those from AC.
source: We note that similar to previous studies, FA and calcium signals from the MGB are smaller than those from AC (Dana et al., 2014; Llano et al., 2009), which may be related to limited alignment of mitochondria-containing neuropil processes or low baseline expression of GCaMP in the MGB, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and inference about possible mechanisms.

claim: LFPs recorded in the AC showed all-or-none response patterns that strongly correlated with the FA signals.
source: To ensure that metabolic or imaging artifacts did not drive the observation of these stochastic population cortical responses, local field potentials (LFPs) were recorded in the AC while simultaneously conducting FA imaging, and the LFPs also showed all-or-none response patterns that strongly correlated with the FA signals (Figure 2F, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from simultaneous LFP recording and FA imaging (Figure 2F).

claim: Stochastic population AC responses were observed in brain slices prepared using a different anesthetic (isoflurane) without transcardiac perfusion in a different laboratory using a biphasic stimulator vs. monophasic stimulator.
source: We also observed stochastic population AC responses in brain slices prepared using a different anesthetic (isoflurane) without transcardiac perfusion in a different laboratory using a biphasic stimulator vs. monophasic stimulator (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting that the stochastic responses were not specific to a particular slice preparation or stimulation technique.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a different laboratory setup (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and inference about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Stimulus-evoked calcium signals of a small population of layer 4 cells showed that a similar population of layer 4 cells was activated with each population ON response and that population OFF responses were associated with an absence of layer four responses.
source: Looking more closely at the activity of cortical layer 4 cells, the stimulus-evoked calcium signals of a small population of layer 4 cells following IC stimulation showed that a similar population layer 4 cells was activated with each population ON response and that population OFF responses were associated with an absence of layer four responses. For instance, all neurons ceased to respond during stimuli # 9 and 11 (Figure 2G, rose ribbons, Figure 2—source data 4) and (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging of layer 4 cells (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).

claim: Whole-cell recordings of layer 4 cells during population ON responses revealed a plateau of depolarization upon which rode several action potentials, resembling previously described UP states.
source: Whole-cell recordings of layer 4 cells during population ON population responses revealed a plateau of depolarization upon which rode several action potentials (Figure 2H, green box, Figure 2—source data 5), resembling previously described UP states (Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Rigas and Castro-Alamancos, 2007; Fanselow and Connors, 2010), which was supported by the bimodal distribution shown by the post stimulus membrane potential of such layer 4 cells during population ON cortical responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 2—figure supplement 6—source data 1, see, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 6) and citations to previous studies describing UP states.

claim: IC stimulation produces stochastic population responses in the AC, and these population responses are stereotyped and represent stimulus-induced UP states.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that IC stimulation produces stochastic population responses in the AC, and that these population responses are stereotyped and represent stimulus-induced UP states.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Population ON/OFF cortical responses occurred only after electrical stimulation of IC, and not by the direct stimulation of MGB or the subcortical white matter.
source: Population ON/OFF cortical responses occurred only after electrical stimulation of IC, and not by the direct stimulation of MGB or the subcortical white matter (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2, Kruskal-Wallis: p=0.001, pairwise comparison: p=0.023 for IC vs. MGB or subcortical white matter and p=1 for MGB vs. subcortical white matter, Dunn's post hoc test, n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing stimulation at different sites (Figure 3B, 3D) and statistical analysis.

claim: The percentage of population ON cortical responses increased with increasing amplitude of the stimulating current.
source: Similar to the in vivo data, the percentage of population ON cortical responses increased with increasing amplitude of the stimulating current (Figure 3E, Figure 3—source data 4, RM-ANOVA: *F(3,9)=9.7, p=0.003, pairwise comparison: *p=0.009 for 50 vs. 150–200 μA, *p=0.008 for 50 vs. 250–300 μA, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 4 slices from four animals), which was consistent with the in vivo results (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between stimulating current amplitude and response frequency (Figure 3E) and statistical analysis.

claim: There was a log-linear relationship between the FA signals of either IC or MGB and the stimulating current amplitude.
source: Moreover, while there was a log-linear relationship between the FA signals of either IC or MGB and the stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 5, R2 = 0.68, p=2.2×10−19 for IC and R2 = 0.53, p=3.3×10−13 for MGB), this relationship was lost between the cortical responses and stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F, Figure 3—source data 5, R2 = 0.004, p=0.6), suggesting that the magnitude of the cortical response is not predictable from stimulus amplitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between FA signals and stimulating current amplitude (Figure 3F) and statistical analysis, with inference about predictability.

claim: Bath application of gabazine (SR-95531, 200 nM), the GABAΑ-R blocker, was able to retrieve all missing cortical responses compared to control.
source: Under simultaneous FA imaging and IC stimulation, gabazine perfusion was able to retrieve all missing cortical responses compared to control (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 1 and 2, Kruskal-Wallis: p=2.5×10−7, pairwise comparison: p=5.08×10−4 for gabazine vs. control, p=4.1×10−7 for gabazine vs. wash, and p=0.34 for control vs. wash, Dunn's post hoc test, n = 14 trials obtained from five animals), which suggested that the population OFF cortical responses were driven by inhibitory inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4B, 4C) and statistical analysis.

claim: Layer 4 cells demonstrated a surge of evoked post-stimulus IPSCs during population ON cortical responses only.
source: Consistent with the previous finding that stimulation of the IC evoked a post-stimulus UP-states activity in layer 4 cells during the population ON cortical responses only (Figure 2H; Fanselow and Connors, 2010; Haider et al., 2006), layer 4 cells demonstrated a surge of evoked post-stimulus IPSCs during population ON cortical responses only (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4D) and citations to previous studies.

claim: MGB cells showed evoked post-stimulus IPSCs following every trial of IC stimulation during population ON and population OFF cortical responses.
source: In contrast, MGB cells showed evoked post-stimulus IPSCs following every trial of IC stimulation during population ON and population OFF cortical responses (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4E).

claim: Evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCs in layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses.
source: Quantitatively, while these evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCS in the layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 3, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test: p=0.006 for IPSCs, n = 10 cells from four animals and p=0.036 for EPSCs, n = 6 cells from four animals), the evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 4, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.011 for IPSCs, n = 20 cells from seven animals and p=0.56 for EPSCs, n = 14 cells from four animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4F, 4G) and statistical analysis.

claim: The evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges.
source: Quantitatively, while these evoked cortical post-stimulus IPSCs and EPSCS in the layer 4 cells were significantly smaller during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 3, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test: p=0.006 for IPSCs, n = 10 cells from four animals and p=0.036 for EPSCs, n = 6 cells from four animals), the evoked post-stimulus IPSCs in the MGB cells were larger during population OFF compared to population ON cortical responses, with no difference in the net excitatory transferred charges (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 4, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.011 for IPSCs, n = 20 cells from seven animals and p=0.56 for EPSCs, n = 14 cells from four animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 4G) and statistical analysis.

claim: MGB cells receive more inhibition during population OFF cortical responses with no change in excitation.
source: These findings suggest that MGB cells receive more inhibition during population OFF cortical responses with no change in excitation, which led us to hypothesize that MGB activity could be modulated by inhibitory inputs during the population OFF cortical responses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: Specific injection of gabazine into the MGB in the aCTC slice was able to significantly increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses.
source: Under simultaneous FA imaging and IC stimulation, the specific injection of gabazine (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) into the MGB in the aCTC slice was able to significantly increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses (Figure 4I and J, Figure 4—source data 5 and 6), indicated by the Δf/f of the evoked cortical FA signals (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 7, RM-ANOVA: F(3,21) = 13.9, p=3.17×10−5, pairwise comparison: *p=5.9×10−5, 1.5 × 10−4, 0.0026 for gabazine in MGB vs. control, wash, and gabazine in AC, respectively, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 8 slices from seven animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4I, 4J, 4K) and statistical analysis.

claim: Selective gabazine injection into the AC did not increase the percentage of population ON cortical responses.
source: In contrast, the same effect was not observed after selective gabazine injection into the AC (Figure 4K, Figure 4—source data 7, RM-ANOVA: F(3,21) = 13.9, pairwise comparison: p=0.73 and 1.0 for gabazine in AC vs. control and wash, respectively, Bonferroni post hoc test, n = 8 slices from seven animals), consistent with data obtained from the whole-cell recording of layer 4 cells (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 4K) and statistical analysis.

claim: Population OFF cortical responses could be driven by thalamic inhibition.
source: Accordingly, these data confirmed that the population OFF cortical responses could be driven by thalamic inhibition.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The mean peak latencies of IPSCs and EPSCs received by MGB cells showed no difference during population ON and population OFF cortical responses.
source: Although the mean peak latencies of IPSCs and EPSCs received by MGB cells showed no difference during population ON and population OFF cortical responses (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—source data 1, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.28, n = 20 cells from seven animals for IPSCs and paired t-test: t(12) = −0.72, p=0.48, n = 14 cells from four animals for EPSCs), the cumulative distribution function showed that some MGB cells (~50% of the recorded cells) received earlier IPSCs during population OFF cortical responses (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 5A, 5B) and statistical analysis.

claim: Some MGB cells (~50% of the recorded cells) received earlier IPSCs during population OFF cortical responses.
source: Although the mean peak latencies of IPSCs and EPSCs received by MGB cells showed no difference during population ON and population OFF cortical responses (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—source data 1, paired sample Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test: p=0.28, n = 20 cells from seven animals for IPSCs and paired t-test: t(12) = −0.72, p=0.48, n = 14 cells from four animals for EPSCs), the cumulative distribution function showed that some MGB cells (~50% of the recorded cells) received earlier IPSCs during population OFF cortical responses (Figure 5C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell recordings (Figure 5C) and statistical analysis.

claim: The variance of the peak latencies of the evoked calcium signals from all thalamic cells was larger during population OFF cortical responses than population ON responses.
source: We observed that the variance of the peak latencies of the evoked calcium signals from all thalamic cells was larger during population OFF cortical responses than population ON responses (Figure 5F, Figure 5—source data 3, paired sample t-test: t(13) = −2.37, *p=0.033, n = 14 paired responses (population ON vs. population OFF) including 339 cells from five animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging (Figure 5F) and statistical analysis.

claim: Synchronous thalamic relay cell activity is required to evoke a cortical population ON response.
source: These data suggest that synchronous thalamic relay cell activity is required to evoke a cortical population ON response, consistent with previous work (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 5 and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: Photoinhibition of corticothalamic layer 6 cells by illumination with 565 nm light resulted in a significant increase in the probability of population ON cortical responses.
source: Photoinhibition of corticothalamic layer 6 cells by illumination with 565 nm light resulted in a significant increase in the probability of population ON cortical responses as indicated by the recovery of the post-stimulus LFP signals from L3/4 compared to the control (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—source data 1, paired t-test: t(15) = −7.06, **p=3.8×10−6, n = 16 trials from four animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulation (Figure 6C, 6D) and statistical analysis.

claim: Illumination of the aCTC slice expressing YFP in layer 6 cells with 565 nm light could not retrieve the population ON cortical responses.
source: A control experiment was done by injecting NTSR1-Cre mice with a virus expressing YFP without the inhibitory opsin. The same illumination of the aCTC slice expressing YFP in layer 6 cells (Figure 6F) with a 565 nm light of could not retrieve the population ON cortical responses (Figure 6G and H, Figure 6—source data 2, paired t-test: t(24) = −1.3, p=0.2, n = 25 trials from five animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control experiment (Figure 6G, 6H) and statistical analysis.

claim: Chemical inhibition of corticothalamic layer 6 cells expressing hM4Di receptors by CNO significantly increased the frequency of population ON cortical responses.
source: Consistent with the previous data, the chemical inhibition of corticothalamic layer 6 cells expressing hM4Di receptors by their chemical actuator, CNO, significantly increased the frequency of population ON cortical responses as indicated by Δf/f of evoked cortical FA signals compared to the control (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2, paired test: t(3) = −3.66, p=0.035, n = 4 trials from four animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemogenetic manipulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, 1D) and statistical analysis.

claim: Perfusion of CNO to the aCTC slices expressing mCherry without DREADDs could not retrieve the population ON cortical responses.
source: The control experiment was done by injecting other NTSR1-Cre mice with a virus expressing mCherry without the DREADDs, and the perfusion of CNO to the aCTC slices taken from these animals could not retrieve the population ON cortical responses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 3, paired test: t(4) = 0.9, p=0.4, n = 5 trials from five animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from a control experiment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E) and statistical analysis.

claim: Blocking of the TRN activity by NBQX significantly increased the probability of population ON cortical events.
source: Blocking of the TRN activity by NBQX, the AMPA-R blocker (Sun et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2010a), which was specifically injected into TRN, significantly increased the probability of population ON cortical events indicated by Δf/f of the evoked cortical FA signals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1—source data 4 and 5, paired test: t(5) = −6.03, **p=5.2×10−4, n = 8 trials from seven animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from pharmacological manipulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, 1H) and statistical analysis.

claim: Photoinhibition of layer 5 cells expressing eNpHR3.0 receptors by illumination with 565 nm light could not retrieve the missing cortical responses.
source: Consistent with the previous data, the photoinhibition of layer 5 cells expressing eNpHR3.0 receptors by illumination with 565 nm light could not retrieve the missing cortical responses, indicated by no recovery of the post-stimulus LFP signals from L3/4 compared to control (no light) (Figure 6K and L, Figure 6—source data 3, paired t-test: t(36) = 0.46, p=0.18, n = 37 trials from four animals), which suggests that the population OFF cortical responses were specifically driven by MGB inhibition through corticothalamic layer 6-TRN pathway.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulation (Figure 6K, 6L) and statistical analysis.

claim: Photoinhibition of GABAergic cells of the IC by illumination with 565 nm light was not able to retrieve the missing cortical responses.
source: Photoinhibition of GABAergic cells of the IC by illumination with 565 nm light was not able to retrieve the missing cortical responses as indicated by no recovery of the post-stimulus LFP signals recorded from L3/4 (Figure 6O and P, Figure 6—source data 4, Paired t-test: t(6) = −1.03, p=0.34, n = 7 trials from five animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulation (Figure 6O, 6P) and statistical analysis.

claim: Population OFF cortical responses were most likely driven by the feedback inhibition of MGB by corticothalamic layer 6 cells via TRN.
source: Accordingly, based on the data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, we conclude that the population OFF cortical responses were most likely driven by the feedback inhibition of MGB by corticothalamic layer 6 cells via TRN.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stochastic population cortical responses were observed in the mouse AC following the presentations of pure tones in vivo or electrical stimulation of the IC in vitro.
source: We observed stochastic population cortical responses in the mouse AC following the presentations of pure tones in vivo or electrical stimulation of the IC in vitro.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Population ON responses were associated with synchronized responses among MGB cells.
source: Population ON responses were associated with synchronized responses among MGB cells, whereas population OFF responses were associated with TRN-mediated inhibition at the level of the MGB, under the control of layer 6 corticothalamic projections.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Population OFF responses were associated with TRN-mediated inhibition at the level of the MGB, under the control of layer 6 corticothalamic projections.
source: Population ON responses were associated with synchronized responses among MGB cells, whereas population OFF responses were associated with TRN-mediated inhibition at the level of the MGB, under the control of layer 6 corticothalamic projections.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental data presented in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: Other inhibitory projections to the MGB from the IC had no impact on the probability of eliciting a population ON response.
source: Other inhibitory projections to the MGB from the IC had no impact on the probability of eliciting a population ON response.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6O, 6P.

claim: It is unlikely that population OFF cortical responses were a sign of cortical adaptation, because adaptation responses are generally characterized by gradual decrease of the response amplitude, rather than the all-or-none responses observed here.
source: It is unlikely that population OFF cortical responses were a sign of cortical adaptation, because adaptation responses are generally characterized by gradual decrease of the response amplitude, rather than the all-or-none responses observed here (Chung et al., 2002; Abolafia et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to previous studies describing adaptation.

claim: Layer 6 corticothalamic neurons gate population activity in the AC via their projections to TRN, which desynchronize MGB neurons.
source: We conclude from these findings that layer 6 corticothalamic neurons gate population activity in the AC via their projections to TRN, which desynchronize MGB neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Previous work has suggested that corticothalamic axons, via the strong inhibition to thalamocortical cells by way of the TRN, control thalamocortical information flow.
source: Previous work has suggested that corticothalamic axons, via the strong inhibition to thalamocortical cells by way of the TRN (Crandall et al., 2015; Olsen et al., 2012; Paz and Huguenard, 2015; Steriade et al., 1996; Guillery and Harting, 2003; McAlonan et al., 2008), control thalamocortical information flow (Destexhe, 2000; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The gating mechanism appears to involve TRN-based desynchronization of thalamocortical neurons rather than diminishing the overall thalamic response.
source: In the current study, the gating mechanism appears to involve TRN-based desynchronization of thalamocortical neurons rather than diminishing the overall thalamic response, which is consistent with previous findings showing that the TRN can desynchronize thalamocortical cells via multiple mechanisms (Pita-Almenar et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and is consistent with previous work cited.

claim: Direct electrical stimulation of the thalamus did not lead to stochastic AC response because direct electrical stimulation is likely to elicit highly synchronous responses among MGB neurons.
source: This explanation is also consistent with our finding that direct electrical stimulation of the thalamus did not lead to stochastic AC response because direct electrical stimulation is likely to elicit highly synchronous responses among MGB neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: It is possible that silencing layer six corticothalamic neurons led to changes in likelihood of activating the AC via intracortical connections of NTSR1-positive neurons.
source: It is also possible that silencing layer six corticothalamic neurons led to changes in likelihood of activating the AC via intracortical connections of NTSR1-positive neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Population OFF cortical responses in the current study were never initiated by the first stimulation of the IC.
source: We also note that population OFF cortical responses in the current study were never initiated by the first stimulation of the IC. Rather they were always elicited by the subsequent IC stimulation, which suggests that population OFF cortical responses occurred only after evoked cortical activity that could change the internal dynamics of the cortical cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the stimulation experiments.

claim: The strong association between the high probability of the OFF cortical responses and the low level of stimulation suggests that cortico-reticulothalamic control of thalamocortical transmission is most likely to be effective when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
source: Moreover, the strong association between the high probability of the OFF cortical responses and the low level of stimulation suggests that cortico-reticulothalamic control of thalamocortical transmission is most likely to be effective when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1F and 3E.

claim: This finding is consistent with the notion that top-down modulation is mostly required for the attentional modulation of weak signals and that highly salient signals rely on bottom-up mechanisms to activate perceptual representations.
source: This finding is consistent with the notion that top-down modulation is mostly required for the attentional modulation of weak signals and that highly salient signals rely on bottom-up mechanisms to activate perceptual representations (reviewed in Asilador and Llano, 2020).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and is consistent with a review cited.

claim: Classical models have viewed sensory processing stations, including the thalamus and cortex, as a series of feedforward, hierarchically organized filters whereby combinations of receptive fields produce increasingly selective feature detectors, culminating in uniquely selective neurons.
source: Classical models have viewed sensory processing stations, including the thalamus and cortex, as a series of feedforward, hierarchically organized filters whereby combinations of receptive fields produce increasingly selective feature detectors, culminating in uniquely selective neurons (Riesenhuber and Poggio, 1999; Vidyasagar and Eysel, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing classical models.

claim: An alternative view is that ascending information is used to create and modify a bank of sensory representations that are recruited depending on behavioral needs, and that conscious perception reflects activation of these pre-wired circuits.
source: An alternative view is that ascending information is used to create and modify a bank of sensory representations that are recruited depending on behavioral needs, and that conscious perception reflects activation of these pre-wired circuits (Ringach, 2009; Llinás, 1994; Mishkin, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies describing an alternative view.

claim: Conscious perception may involve the release of stereotyped patterns of cortical activity.
source: Thus, conscious perception may involve the release of stereotyped patterns of cortical activity.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the alternative view of sensory processing.

claim: One potential role of thalamocortical transmission in this model is to select cortical ensembles rather than impress sensory information upon them.
source: One potential role of thalamocortical transmission in this model is to select cortical ensembles rather than impress sensory information upon them.
evidence: The claim is speculation about the role of thalamocortical transmission.

claim: At the thalamocortical level, sensory inputs activate stereotyped patterns of population cortical activity.
source: Our data suggest that at the thalamocortical level, sensory inputs activate stereotyped patterns of population cortical activity.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A mechanism of TRN-based modification of thalamic synchrony to activate the cortex has been proposed previously.
source: A mechanism of TRN-based modification of thalamic synchrony to activate the cortex has been proposed previously (Saalmann and Kastner, 2011) and is consistent with the finding that synchronized populations of thalamic neurons are required to optimally activate the cortex (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006) and that the TRN is at the heart of a prefrontal cortex-based mechanism to shape cortical activation under changing cognitive demands (Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2006; Wimmer et al., 2015; Yingling and Skinner, 1975).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TRN receives inputs from basal forebrain, amygdala and non-reciprocally linked regions of the thalamus.
source: Further, the TRN receives inputs from basal forebrain, amygdala and non-reciprocally linked regions of the thalamus (Kimura et al., 2007; Lam and Sherman, 2005; Lam and Sherman, 2015; Crabtree et al., 1998; Crabtree and Isaac, 2002; Lee et al., 2010b; Desîlets-Roy et al., 2002; Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2012; Aizenberg et al., 2019), forming an assortment of inputs to potentially modulate TRN, and ultimately select cortical circuits for activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Given the putative role of the TRN in the selection of thalamic, and therefore cortical circuits during sensory perception, one would predict that disruption of TRN activity could lead to uncontrolled release of patterns of cortical activity.
source: Given the putative role of the TRN in the selection of thalamic, and therefore cortical circuits during sensory perception, one would predict that disruption of TRN activity could lead to uncontrolled release of patterns of cortical activity.
evidence: The claim is speculation based on the proposed role of the TRN.

claim: Ample evidence has accumulated to suggest that schizophrenia, a disease characterized by the presence of auditory hallucinations, involves disruption of the TRN.
